title: Floods and climate: emerging perspectives for flood risk assessment and management

venue.name: Natural hazards and earth system sciences

abstract: Abstract. Flood estimation and flood management have traditionally been the domain of hydrologists, water resources engineers and statisticians, and disciplinary approaches abound. Dominant views have been shaped; one example is the catchment perspective: floods are formed and influenced by the interaction of local, catchment-specific characteristics, such as meteorology, topography and geology. These traditional views have been beneficial, but they have a narrow framing. In this paper we contrast traditional views with broader perspectives that are emerging from an improved understanding of the climatic context of floods. We come to the following conclusions: (1) extending the traditional system boundaries (local catchment, recent decades, hydrological/hydraulic processes) opens up exciting possibilities for better understanding and improved tools for flood risk assessment and management. (2) Statistical approaches in flood estimation need to be complemented by the search for the causal mechanisms and dominant processes in the atmosphere, catchment and river system that leave their fingerprints on flood characteristics. (3) Natural climate variability leads to time-varying flood characteristics, and this variation may be partially quantifiable and predictable, with the perspective of dynamic, climate-informed flood risk management. (4) Efforts are needed to fully account for factors that contribute to changes in all three risk components (hazard, exposure, vulnerability) and to better understand the interactions between society and floods. (5) Given the global scale and societal importance, we call for the organization of an international multidisciplinary collaboration and data-sharing initiative to further understand the links between climate and flooding and to advance flood research.
problem: Traditional flood risk assessment is limited by a narrow framing that treats floods as local, random, and stationary events, thereby failing to account for the broader causal influence of global climate mechanisms, long-term perspectives, and time-varying natural variability.
method: The paper proposes a method for developing process-based flooding scenarios by partitioning the observed flood record by climatic cause and re-sampling distinctive segments to simulate flood behavior under plausible projected climatic shifts.
task: The task is to contrast traditional, narrowly-framed approaches to flood risk assessment and management with emerging perspectives that incorporate a broader understanding of the climatic context of floods.
innovation: This paper contrasts traditional, narrow views of flood risk with emerging perspectives that advocate for extending system boundaries in space (global), time (long-term), and process (causal mechanisms) to improve flood risk assessment and management.
